````go
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	require.Contains(t, body, "Logged out.")

	resp, _ = fetchPage(t, base+"/", cookie)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusSeeOther, resp.StatusCode)
	require.Equal(t, "/login", resp.Header.Get("Location"))
}

// TestServer_WebFormsCSRF drives the refusal through the real binary: a form
// post with a live session but no token — or another token — is a 403 in the
// one error shape, and the store is untouched, which the API's own list
// confirms.
func TestServer_WebFormsCSRF(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	srv := startServer(t)
	defer srv.stop(t)

	base := "http://" + srv.addr

	resp := postJSON(t, base+"/api/v1/auth/register", `{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}`, nil)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusCreated, resp.StatusCode)
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())

	resp = postJSON(t, base+"/api/v1/auth/login", `{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"correct horse battery staple"}`, nil)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	cookies := resp.Cookies()
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	require.Len(t, cookies, 1, "login sets the session cookie")
	cookie := cookies[0]

	// Render a page first: the session then holds a token, so both refusals
	// below are real compares, not an empty-session shortcut.
	resp, _ = fetchPage(t, base+"/", cookie)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)

	// No token: refused before the handler, in the house shape.
	resp = postForm(t, base+"/tasks", url.Values{"title": {"buy milk"}}, cookie)
	body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusForbidden, resp.StatusCode)
	require.JSONEq(t, `{"code":"forbidden","message":"invalid CSRF token"}`, string(body))

	// A wrong token is the same answer.
	resp = postForm(t, base+"/tasks", url.Values{
		"csrf_token": {"not-the-session-token"},
		"title":      {"buy milk"},
	}, cookie)
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusForbidden, resp.StatusCode)

	// Nothing was written: the API's own list is empty.
	resp, apiBody := fetchPage(t, base+"/api/v1/tasks", cookie)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	require.JSONEq(t, `{"tasks":[]}`, apiBody)
}

// TestServer_StaticAssets proves the embed travels in the binary: the
// process serves the design system's stylesheet out of its own executable —
// the temp directory holds only the database and the log, and the CSS is
// compiled in — with the cache policy's validators, and the conditional GET
// is the 304. The URL is the one the page's own output named, so the link
// and the asset cannot drift apart, and nothing below main could prove the
// deployable artifact carries the design system; this is that proof at the
// process level, the way the page tests prove the mount.
func TestServer_StaticAssets(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	srv := startServer(t)
	defer srv.stop(t)

	base := "http://" + srv.addr

	resp, page := fetchPage(t, base+"/login")
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	link := stylesheetLink.FindStringSubmatch(page)
	require.Len(t, link, 2, "the page links its stylesheet")

	resp, css := fetchPage(t, base+link[1])
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	require.Contains(t, resp.Header.Get("Content-Type"), "text/css")
	require.Equal(t, "no-cache", resp.Header.Get("Cache-Control"))
	tag := resp.Header.Get("ETag")
	require.NotEmpty(t, tag, "the stylesheet carries a validator")
	require.Contains(t, css, ":root")

	// The second visit is a revalidation: the tag travels back, the answer
	// is a 304, and the body is not sent again.
	req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+link[1], nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	req.Header.Set("If-None-Match", tag)
	resp, err = http.DefaultClient.Do(req) // #nosec G107 -- the test's own listener address
	require.NoError(t, err)
	body, err := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusNotModified, resp.StatusCode)
	require.Empty(t, body, "a 304 carries no body")
}

// TestServer_AdminKeyBootstrap drives the chapter's boot path through the
// real binary: TODO_ADMIN_KEY seeds the admin account, the ordinary login
// route opens it, the admin gate the profile routes carry accepts it, a wrong
// key does not, and the key is in no record the boot wrote.
func TestServer_AdminKeyBootstrap(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	const key = "todo-admin-key-that-never-reaches-the-log"
	srv := startServer(t,
		"TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=Admin@Example.COM",
		"TODO_ADMIN_KEY="+key,
	)
	defer srv.stop(t)

	base := "http://" + srv.addr

	// The ordinary login opens the seeded account: the bootstrap adds no
	// second way in, it only makes sure the first one has an admin behind it.
	resp := postJSON(t, base+"/api/v1/auth/login",
		fmt.Sprintf(`{"email":"admin@example.com","password":%q}`, key), nil)
	require.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode)
	cookies := resp.Cookies()
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	require.Len(t, cookies, 1, "a login sets the session cookie")

	// The admin gate answers the seeded account, so the profiles are
	// reachable without the CLI ever running.
	req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, base+"/debug/pprof/", nil)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	req.AddCookie(cookies[0])
	profiles, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
	require.NoError(t, err)
	require.NoError(t, profiles.Body.Close())
	assert.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, profiles.StatusCode)

	// A wrong key is a wrong password: the stored credential is a hash of the
	// key, so nothing else opens the account.
	resp = postJSON(t, base+"/api/v1/auth/login",
		`{"email":"admin@example.com","password":"not the key"}`, nil)
	require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
	assert.Equal(t, http.StatusUnauthorized, resp.StatusCode)

	// The boot's records say what it ensured and never what it ensured it
	// with: the key is in neither sink.
	logData, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join(srv.dir, "todo.log")) // #nosec G304 -- the test's own temp path
	require.NoError(t, err)
	assert.Contains(t, string(logData), `"msg":"admin credential ensured"`)
	assert.Contains(t, string(logData), `"created":true`)
	for _, sink := range []struct {
		name string
		data string
	}{
		{"stderr", srv.stderr.String()},
		{"the log file", string(logData)},
	} {
		assert.NotContains(t, sink.data, key, "%s carries the key", sink.name)
	}
}

// TestServer_AdminKeyFile drives the file variant through the real binary: a
// file every account can read is refused before the server starts, and the
// same file at 0600 boots and opens the account — with the trailing newline
// the file was written with trimmed off the key.
func TestServer_AdminKeyFile(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	dir := t.TempDir()
	path := filepath.Join(dir, "admin-key")
	const key = "todo-admin-key-from-a-file"
	require.NoError(t, os.WriteFile(path, []byte(key+"\n"), 0o644)) // #nosec G306 -- the permissive mode is the case under test
	require.NoError(t, os.Chmod(path, 0o644))                       // #nosec G302 -- the permissive mode is the case under test

	t.Run("a world-readable file is refused", func(t *testing.T) {
		// The boot must fail, not serve: a credential the process could not
		// verify was private is a credential it must not use. The context is
		// the deadline a boot that wrongly started would be killed at, so a
		// regression fails the assertions instead of hanging the suite.
		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
		defer cancel()

		// #nosec G204 -- binPath is built by TestMain from this package's own
		// source, and the arguments are test-authored.
		cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, binPath, "--listen", "127.0.0.1:0")
		cmd.Env = []string{
			"PATH=" + os.Getenv("PATH"),
			"TODO_DB=" + filepath.Join(dir, "todo.db"),
			"TODO_LOG=" + filepath.Join(dir, "todo.log"),
			"TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com",
			"TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE=" + path,
		}
		out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()
		require.Error(t, err, "the boot must fail; output:\n%s", out)
		assert.Contains(t, string(out), "0644", "the refusal names the mode it found")
		assert.NotContains(t, string(out), key, "the refusal does not echo the key")

		// The refusal runs before anything opens a file: a boot that cannot
		// honor the operator's secret leaves nothing behind — not the log it
		// would have written to, not the database.
		_, err = os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, "todo.log"))
		assert.True(t, os.IsNotExist(err), "the refused boot created a log file")
		_, err = os.Stat(filepath.Join(dir, "todo.db"))
		assert.True(t, os.IsNotExist(err), "the refused boot created a database")
	})

	t.Run("a private file boots", func(t *testing.T) {
		require.NoError(t, os.Chmod(path, 0o600))

		srv := startServer(t,
			"TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com",
			"TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE="+path,
		)
		defer srv.stop(t)

		resp := postJSON(t, "http://"+srv.addr+"/api/v1/auth/login",
			fmt.Sprintf(`{"email":"admin@example.com","password":%q}`, key), nil)
		require.NoError(t, resp.Body.Close())
		assert.Equal(t, http.StatusOK, resp.StatusCode, "the file's key opens the account, newline trimmed")
	})
}
````

## `cmd/todo-server/main.go`

````go
// Command todo-server is the todo application's HTTP server: the wiring
// around internal/api and internal/web — configuration, the process logger,
// the store's lifecycle, signals, and the exit code. The API routes live in
// internal/api, the server-rendered pages in internal/web, and main composes
// both onto one echo instance so they share the middleware stack, the
// session, and the store.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"net/http"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"
	"time"

	"golang.org/x/term"

	"todo/internal/api"
	"todo/internal/auth"
	"todo/internal/config"
	"todo/internal/logging"
	"todo/internal/secret"
	"todo/internal/store"
	"todo/internal/telemetry"
	"todo/internal/version"
	"todo/internal/web"
)

// shutdownTimeout bounds the drain: how long Shutdown waits for in-flight
// requests before giving up. Chapter 30 chose five seconds — "longer than
// anything this server serves" — and chapter 48's numbers make that wrong:
// the stack arms a ten-second deadline on every request (internal/api's
// requestTimeout), so a request that was in flight when the signal arrived
// can have its whole deadline left to run, and a five-second drain cuts work
// the server would still have served — and exits non-zero, which a
// supervisor reads as a failed stop. The budget is that deadline plus a
// five-second margin for the store's checkpoint and the process's last
// records; the unit's TimeoutStopSec outlasts both.
const shutdownTimeout = 15 * time.Second

// flushTimeout bounds the tracer's last export, and it is deliberately not
// the drain's budget: a batch export that has not finished in five seconds
// is not going to, and the requests were served either way.
const flushTimeout = 5 * time.Second

// The API's general documentation, as swaggo annotations. swag init reads
// this block — it has to be a comment group of its own — for the spec's
// title, version, and tags; the per-handler annotations live beside the
// handlers they describe, in internal/api. The generated spec and the
// Swagger UI that serves it are internal/api/docs.

//	@title			Todo API
//	@version		1.0
//	@description	The todo application's HTTP surface: the task CRUD routes
//	@description	and the auth routes that gate them.
//	@description
//	@description	The task routes require a session: log in through
//	@description	`POST /api/v1/auth/login` first, and the cookie it sets
//	@description	carries the identity on every following request. Every task
//	@description	is scoped to the authenticated user, so a task another user
//	@description	owns answers exactly what a missing task answers.
//	@description
//	@description		Every failure leaves in one shape — `code`, `message`, and,
//	@description		on a validation failure, `fields`. The responses named per
//	@description		operation are the ones its handler decides; the stack's own
//	@description		failures can arrive on any route in the same shape: 413 for
//	@description		a body over 64 KiB, 500 for an internal error, 504 for a
//	@description		request past its ten-second deadline.
//	@tag.name			tasks
//	@tag.description	The task CRUD surface. Every route requires a session and is scoped to the caller.
//	@tag.name			auth
//	@tag.description	Registration, login, and logout — the routes an anonymous caller can reach.
//	@tag.name			health
//	@tag.description	Liveness and readiness probes for supervisors, not clients.

// main is the process's only job: exit with run's code.
func main() {
	os.Exit(run())
}

// run starts the server and returns the process's exit code: 0 after a clean
// shutdown, 1 after printing the one error line. It reads os.Args and writes
// to os.Stderr, so the real binary and the integration test run the same
// function.
func run() int {
	// A first interrupt or SIGTERM cancels ctx: the server then stops
	// accepting and drains within shutdownTimeout. stop is called at that
	// point rather than only deferred: with the handler unregistered, a
	// second signal reaches the process with the default disposition and
	// kills it — the operator's way out of a drain that will not finish.
	// main's os.Exit skips the defer, but the process is leaving anyway.
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	// The server has exactly one flag, so the stdlib flag package is
	// enough; cobra stays where the command tree is. A parse error exits 2
	// with the usage, the convention Go's own tools follow.
	listenFlag := flag.String("listen", "", "listen address; overrides $TODO_LISTEN and the 127.0.0.1:8080 default")
	flag.Parse()

	cfg, err := config.Load(os.Getenv, "")
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	// The --listen flag is the last word, resolved through the same rule
	// the environment and the default went through.
	cfg.Listen = config.Listen(os.Getenv, *listenFlag)

	// The admin bootstrap's key arrives through internal/secret, which
	// returns a value that cannot be printed: the key never enters Config —
	// a Config is a value callers may log — and never reaches a record. The
	// loader enforces the file's mode bits where the environment names a
	// file, and refuses a configuration that names two sources for one
	// credential. It runs before anything opens a file — the log included —
	// so a boot that refuses the operator's secret leaves nothing behind,
	// and the process never starts a logger it would only use to report the
	// refusal.
	adminKey, err := secret.Load(os.Getenv, config.EnvAdminKey, config.EnvAdminKeyFile)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	if !adminKey.IsEmpty() && cfg.AdminEmail == "" {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "todo-server: the admin key is set but TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL is not; a credential has to name an account")
		return 1
	}

	// The TTY decision belongs here, where the real stderr is: a terminal
	// gets tint's human-readable records, anything else JSON. The file sink
	// is JSON either way.
	isTTY := term.IsTerminal(int(os.Stderr.Fd()))
	logger, closer, err := logging.New(os.Stderr, isTTY, cfg.LogPath, slog.LevelInfo)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	defer func() {
		// The process is leaving; a close error cannot change the exit
		// code and has nowhere better to go, so it is discarded
		// explicitly, like the CLI's.
		_ = closer.Close()
	}()

	// A canceled boot aborts before serving: NewTursoStore applies the
	// embedded migrations under ctx, so a signal during startup stops there.
	st, err := store.NewTursoStore(ctx, cfg.DBPath)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}

	// The trace pipeline and the metrics registry, built before the server
	// so the stack has them from the first request. The provider's off mode
	// (no endpoint configured) costs a small allocation per span and
	// exports nothing; with an endpoint, the deferred Shutdown below is
	// what flushes the batch processor's last batch before the process
	// leaves.
	tp, err := telemetry.NewTracerProvider(ctx, cfg.OTelEndpoint, logger)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	defer func() {
		// The flush gets its own, smaller budget: a batch export that has
		// not finished in flushTimeout is not going to, and a flush that
		// fails is recorded rather than fatal — the requests were served,
		// and losing the last spans is telemetry's problem, not the
		// process's.
		shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), flushTimeout)
		defer cancel()
		if err := tp.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
			logger.Error("telemetry shutdown failed", "err", err)
		}
	}()

	// The registry the scrape endpoint serves: the runtime's and the
	// process's collectors, on top of which api.New registers the request
	// metrics.
	reg := telemetry.NewRegistry()

	// The auth material shares the store's database handle: one process, one
	// pool, one close. The session store sweeps its expired rows once, here
	// at boot — scs never does, and an expired row is otherwise only refused
	// by the expiry predicate, never removed. A sweep that fails is logged
	// and boot continues: readiness is where a broken database is reported,
	// and a boot that refuses to start over a cleanup would be a worse
	// trade.
	sqlDB := st.DB()
	sessionStore := auth.NewSessionStore(sqlDB)
	if n, err := sessionStore.DeleteExpired(ctx); err != nil {
		logger.Error("session sweep failed", "err", err)
	} else if n > 0 {
		logger.Info("expired sessions removed", "count", n)
	}

	sessions := api.NewSessionManager(sessionStore)

	// The auth service is built once and handed to both surfaces: the API's
	// auth routes and the pages' login form check the same credentials
	// against the same users table and record to the same trail.
	authn := auth.NewService(sqlDB)

	// The bootstrap runs before the server accepts a request, so the first
	// login finds the credential. A failure is a boot failure: the operator
	// set a secret and the process cannot honor it, and a server that came
	// up anyway would look healthy and be wrong. What the boot ensured is
	// recorded; what it ensured it with is not — the key is not an
	// attribute, a message, or a format string anywhere in this process.
	if !adminKey.IsEmpty() {
		res, err := authn.BootstrapAdmin(ctx, cfg.AdminEmail, adminKey)
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
			return 1
		}
		logger.Info("admin credential ensured",
			"email", cfg.AdminEmail,
			"created", res.Created, "rotated", res.Rotated, "granted", res.Granted)
	}

	e := api.New(st, authn, sessions, logger, tp, reg)

	// The server-rendered pages mount onto the instance the API just built:
	// one echo, one middleware stack, one session manager, one store. The
	// pages are registered here rather than inside api.New so the API
	// instance — and the OpenAPI coverage test that walks its route table —
	// stays free of page routes that are not API operations.
	web.New(st, authn, sessions, time.Now).Register(e)

	// Start blocks until the server stops, so it runs in its own goroutine
	// and the main goroutine stays free to receive the signal. The channel
	// carries a failure out: Start returns immediately when it cannot bind,
	// and without the select the process would wait for a signal it can
	// never serve.
	// The release stamp is part of the boot record: an operator looking at
	// a running host can read which tag built the binary, without asking
	// the deployment. "dev" on a release host is the honest signal that
	// the binary was built by hand.
	logger.Info("server listening", "addr", cfg.Listen, "version", version.Version)
	serveErr := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { serveErr <- e.Start(cfg.Listen) }()

	select {
	case <-ctx.Done():
		// The first signal has canceled ctx. Unregistering the handler now
		// is what makes a second signal the escape hatch: it reaches the
		// process with the default disposition and ends a drain that will
		// not finish on its own. systemd's own stop is two-stage one level
		// up — SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after TimeoutStopSec — and this is the
		// same shape for an operator at a terminal or in a container.
		stop()
		logger.Info("shutting down")
	case err := <-serveErr:
		// Start failed before any signal arrived: the address is taken or
		// otherwise unusable. ErrServerClosed cannot happen here — nothing
		// has called Shutdown yet.
		if !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
			return 1
		}
	}

	// Shutdown stops accepting, then waits — up to shutdownTimeout — for
	// in-flight requests to finish. A request that outlives the timeout is
	// cut off rather than holding the process open forever.
	shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), shutdownTimeout)
	defer cancel()
	if err := e.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	logger.Info("server stopped")

	// The store closes last: requests still in flight during Shutdown may
	// have been reading from it.
	if err := st.Close(); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	return 0
}
````

## `cmd/todo-tui/main.go`

````go
// Command todo-tui is the todo application's terminal UI: a Bubble Tea
// program over the HTTP API. It signs in like any other API client — the
// session cookie lands in internal/client's jar — and every list, add, and
// complete is one request to the server the CLI's database lives behind. The
// wiring is this file — configuration, the logger, the client, the program —
// and the model lives in internal/tui.
//
// The program's records go to the log file and nowhere else: a full-screen
// app owns the terminal it is drawing on, and a record written to stdout or
// stderr would land inside the frame. main resolves the same log path the
// CLI resolves — $TODO_LOG, else the XDG state default — with --debug-log on
// top for one session's debugging, and the model's commands write their
// failures there.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"

	tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"

	"todo/internal/client"
	"todo/internal/config"
	"todo/internal/logging"
	"todo/internal/tui"
	"todo/internal/version"
)

// main is the process's only job: exit with run's code.
func main() {
	os.Exit(run())
}

// run resolves the configuration, builds the logger and the client, and runs
// the program. It returns the process's exit code: 0 after a clean quit, 1
// after printing the one error line.
func run() int {
	// A first interrupt or SIGTERM cancels ctx: a request in flight — a
	// login, a load — aborts with a context error instead of the process
	// dying mid-call. The program's own exit on a signal is Bubble Tea's —
	// it quits the event loop and restores the terminal — so this context
	// is only the commands'.
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	// Two flags, so the stdlib flag package is still enough — the same
	// choice cmd/todo-server made. A parse error exits 2 with the usage,
	// the convention Go's own tools follow.
	apiFlag := flag.String("api", "", "API base URL; overrides $TODO_API_URL and the "+config.DefaultAPIURL+" default")
	debugLogFlag := flag.String("debug-log", "", "path to the debug log; overrides $TODO_LOG and the XDG state default")
	flag.Parse()

	// The TUI resolves the two settings it needs, each with its own flag on
	// top of the shared precedence rule. It deliberately does not call
	// config.Load: the database path is not the TUI's to resolve, and
	// requiring HOME for a database the TUI never opens would be a promise
	// the binary does not keep.
	apiURL := config.APIURL(os.Getenv, *apiFlag)
	logPath, err := config.LogPath(os.Getenv, *debugLogFlag)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}

	// The logger is the file-only one, and it is built before the program
	// starts: a failure here is printed on the still-normal terminal, and a
	// logger built afterwards could miss the records of the very startup
	// that failed. The level is debug — the file is the TUI's only
	// diagnostic surface, and there is no second run of the session being
	// debugged.
	logger, closer, err := logging.NewFile(logPath, slog.LevelDebug)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	defer func() {
		// The process is leaving; a close error cannot change the exit code
		// and has nowhere better to go, so it is discarded explicitly, like
		// the CLI's.
		_ = closer.Close()
	}()

	// The resolved paths are the first debug record, the CLI's own
	// "why is my data not where I thought" answer, on the TUI's side of the
	// pair. The release stamp rides along: the TUI's only diagnostic surface
	// is this file, and which build wrote it is the first question a bug
	// report asks.
	logger.Debug("config resolved", "api", apiURL, "log", logPath, "version", version.Version)

	c := client.New(apiURL)

	// q and ctrl+c both leave through tea.Quit, and Run returns nil. A
	// SIGINT that reaches the process outside the raw terminal — input is
	// not a TTY — arrives as ErrInterrupted, which is the same request to
	// stop, not a failure. Everything else — a recovered panic, a renderer
	// error — is an error, and the one line and the exit code are the
	// report. Bubble Tea restores the terminal before Run returns it, so
	// this line lands on a usable terminal, and the record lands in the file
	// the session was already writing to.
	if _, err := tui.NewProgram(tui.New(ctx, c, tui.WithLogger(logger))).Run(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, tea.ErrInterrupted) {
		logger.Error("todo-tui exited with an error", "err", err)
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	return 0
}
````


## `cmd/todo/integration_test.go`

````go
// The black-box tests: the real binary TestMain built, run through
// exec.Command with a deliberately bare environment. Everything a user
// sees — stdout, stderr, exit codes — is what these tests read; no package
// under internal/ is called directly.
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"encoding/json"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
	"regexp"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
	"testing"
	"time"

	"github.com/google/uuid"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/assert"
	"github.com/stretchr/testify/require"

	"todo/internal/task"
)

// binaryEnv is the whole environment the black-box tests give the binary:
// PATH, so the process starts, and the two variables that pin the CLI's two
// paths. HOME and the XDG variables are absent on purpose: TODO_DB and
// TODO_LOG are the app's own overrides, and with them set the binary must
// not need either.
func binaryEnv(dbPath string) []string {
	return []string{
		"PATH=" + os.Getenv("PATH"),
		"TODO_DB=" + dbPath,
		"TODO_LOG=" + dbPath + ".log",
	}
}

// binaryResult is one black-box run: the two captured streams and the exit
// code. A non-zero code is a result to assert on, not a test failure.
type binaryResult struct {
	stdout string
	stderr string
	code   int
}

// runBinary runs TestMain's binary with the given environment and returns
// what the process printed and how it exited.
func runBinary(t *testing.T, env []string, args ...string) binaryResult {
	t.Helper()
	return runBinaryAt(t, binPath, env, args...)
}

// runBinaryAt runs the binary at bin — TestMain's or one a test built for
// itself — with the given environment and returns what the process printed
// and how it exited.
func runBinaryAt(t *testing.T, bin string, env []string, args ...string) binaryResult {
	t.Helper()
	// #nosec G204 -- bin is built by TestMain or by the calling test from
	// this package's own source, and args are test-authored literals.
	cmd := exec.Command(bin, args...)
	cmd.Env = env
	var stdout, stderr bytes.Buffer
	cmd.Stdout, cmd.Stderr = &stdout, &stderr
	err := cmd.Run()
	code := 0
	if err != nil {
		var exitErr *exec.ExitError
		require.ErrorAs(t, err, &exitErr, "todo %s", strings.Join(args, " "))
		code = exitErr.ExitCode()
	}
	return binaryResult{stdout: stdout.String(), stderr: stderr.String(), code: code}
}

// wireTask is the test's own copy of the --json contract: the seven keys
// chapter 27 documented. Owning the shape here is the point of a black-box
// test — a renamed key fails this struct even though no code in the module
// moved.
type wireTask struct {
	ID       string     `json:"id"`
	Title    string     `json:"title"`
	Status   string     `json:"status"`
	Priority int        `json:"priority"`
	Due      *time.Time `json:"due"`
	Tags     []string   `json:"tags"`
	Version  int        `json:"version"`
}

// TestBinary_RoundTrip is the black-box happy path: the id add prints is
// the handle done takes, list reflects the change, and stats --json counts
// it. Everything travels through the process boundary exactly as a shell
// script would use it.
func TestBinary_RoundTrip(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	env := binaryEnv(filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db"))

	add := runBinary(t, env, "add", "buy milk")
	require.Equal(t, 0, add.code, "add failed: %s", add.stderr)
	id, err := uuid.Parse(strings.TrimSpace(add.stdout))
	require.NoError(t, err, "add prints the id it assigned, got %q", add.stdout)

	done := runBinary(t, env, "done", id.String())
	require.Equal(t, 0, done.code, "done failed: %s", done.stderr)
	assert.Empty(t, done.stdout, "the human done reports nothing on success")

	list := runBinary(t, env, "list")
	require.Equal(t, 0, list.code, "list failed: %s", list.stderr)
	assert.Contains(t, list.stdout, "buy milk")
	assert.Contains(t, list.stdout, "Done")

	// --json is where the status and version can be read exactly: the human
	// table is for eyes, the JSON is for this test.
	jsonList := runBinary(t, env, "list", "--json")
	require.Equal(t, 0, jsonList.code, "list --json failed: %s", jsonList.stderr)
	var got wireTask
	require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal([]byte(jsonList.stdout), &got), "one task, one line: %q", jsonList.stdout)
	assert.Equal(t, id.String(), got.ID)
	assert.Equal(t, "Done", got.Status)
	assert.Equal(t, 2, got.Version, "done bumps the version")

	stats := runBinary(t, env, "stats", "--json")
	require.Equal(t, 0, stats.code, "stats failed: %s", stats.stderr)
	assert.JSONEq(t, `{"total":1,"done":1,"pending":0}`, stats.stdout)
}

// TestBinary_AddDueTomorrow checks that the relative word survives the
// process boundary: `add --due tomorrow` goes in, and the due date that
// comes back out of `list --json` is the domain's own ParseDue answer for
// "tomorrow". The date is computed on both sides of the run, so a midnight
// crossing between the command's time.Now and the test's is accepted rather
// than flaky.
func TestBinary_AddDueTomorrow(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	env := binaryEnv(filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db"))

	before, err := task.ParseDue("tomorrow", time.Now())
	require.NoError(t, err)

	add := runBinary(t, env, "add", "call mom", "--due", "tomorrow")
	require.Equal(t, 0, add.code, "add failed: %s", add.stderr)

	after, err := task.ParseDue("tomorrow", time.Now())
	require.NoError(t, err)

	out := runBinary(t, env, "list", "--json")
	require.Equal(t, 0, out.code, "list --json failed: %s", out.stderr)
	var got wireTask
	require.NoError(t, json.Unmarshal([]byte(out.stdout), &got))
	require.NotNil(t, got.Due, "the task has a due date")
	assert.True(t, got.Due.Equal(before) || got.Due.Equal(after),
		"due = %s, want %s or %s (midnight may cross mid-test)", got.Due, before, after)
}

// TestBinary_ErrorExit pins the error contract at the process level: exit
// code 1, the message on stderr, and not one byte on stdout. The binary is
// built with -cover, so an unset GOCOVERDIR adds the runtime's warning to
// stderr; the assertion matches the message rather than the whole stream,
// while the stdout half of the contract stays exact.
func TestBinary_ErrorExit(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	env := binaryEnv(filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db"))

	res := runBinary(t, env, "done", "not-a-uuid")
	assert.Equal(t, 1, res.code, "a bad id is a failure")
	assert.Empty(t, res.stdout, "the error goes to stderr, not stdout")
	assert.Contains(t, res.stderr, `invalid id "not-a-uuid"`)
}

// TestBinary_Coverage is the cross-process coverage check: the binary was
// built with -cover, so running it with GOCOVERDIR set leaves counter data
// in the directory, and `go tool covdata percent` reads it back. This is
// coverage of the CLI as a real process, collected through the environment
// variable alone — not coverage of the test binary.
func TestBinary_Coverage(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	covDir := t.TempDir()
	env := append(binaryEnv(filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db")), "GOCOVERDIR="+covDir)

	// Three ordinary commands in three processes; covdata reads every
	// counter file the directory holds, so the report below is their
	// merged view.
	require.Equal(t, 0, runBinary(t, env, "add", "buy milk").code)
	require.Equal(t, 0, runBinary(t, env, "list").code)
	require.Equal(t, 0, runBinary(t, env, "stats").code)

	// #nosec G204 -- the tool is a literal; covDir is the temp directory
	// this test just made.
	out, err := exec.Command("go", "tool", "covdata", "percent", "-i="+covDir).CombinedOutput()
	if err != nil {
		t.Skipf("go tool covdata unavailable: %v\n%s", err, out)
	}
	t.Logf("go tool covdata percent:\n%s", out)

	for _, pkg := range []string{"todo/cmd/todo", "todo/internal/cli"} {
		re := regexp.MustCompile(regexp.QuoteMeta(pkg) + `\s+coverage: ([\d.]+)% of statements`)
		m := re.FindStringSubmatch(string(out))
		require.NotNil(t, m, "no coverage line for %s:\n%s", pkg, out)
		pct, err := strconv.ParseFloat(m[1], 64)
		require.NoError(t, err)
		assert.Positive(t, pct, "%s ran no statements", pkg)
	}
}

// TestBinary_Version is the version contract: the release stamps the tag
// into the binary with -ldflags -X and the binary reports it. The two builds
// are the two halves — the injected stamp, and the honest default every
// plain `go build` carries — and both must answer without a database, which
// is the one thing `todo version` may not need.
func TestBinary_Version(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	// TestMain's binary is what `go build ./cmd/todo` produces, version-wise:
	// -cover instruments it, but no ldflags reach it, so the default must
	// come out and no store may be opened to print it.
	dbPath := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db")
	plain := runBinary(t, binaryEnv(dbPath), "version")
	require.Equal(t, 0, plain.code, "version failed: %s", plain.stderr)
	assert.Equal(t, "dev\n", plain.stdout, "a build without a stamp reports the honest default")
	assert.NoFileExists(t, dbPath, "version answers without opening a store")

	// The stamped build uses the release's own invocation: -X names
	// internal/version's variable, the same string .goreleaser.yaml passes.
	// The test spells the import path out rather than sharing a constant
	// with the code, because the path is the contract — a rename that moved
	// the stamp would fail here exactly as it would fail the release.
	stamped := buildStampedBinary(t, "v9.9.9-test")

	env := binaryEnv(filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo.db"))
	res := runBinaryAt(t, stamped, env, "version")
	require.Equal(t, 0, res.code, "stamped version failed: %s", res.stderr)
	assert.Equal(t, "v9.9.9-test\n", res.stdout)

	json := runBinaryAt(t, stamped, env, "version", "--json")
	require.Equal(t, 0, json.code, "version --json failed: %s", json.stderr)
	assert.JSONEq(t, `{"version":"v9.9.9-test"}`, json.stdout)
}

// buildStampedBinary builds cmd/todo with the release's ldflags shape and
// returns the binary's path. `go test` runs the suite with cmd/todo as the
// working directory, so `.` is the package GoReleaser's main field names.
func buildStampedBinary(t *testing.T, version string) string {
	t.Helper()
	bin := filepath.Join(t.TempDir(), "todo")
	// #nosec G204 -- the command is a literal; the stamp and the output
	// path are test-authored.
	cmd := exec.Command("go", "build", "-o", bin,
		"-ldflags", "-X todo/internal/version.Version="+version, ".")
	cmd.Stderr = os.Stderr
	require.NoError(t, cmd.Run(), "build with the release's ldflags")
	return bin
}
````


## `cmd/todo/main.go`

````go
// Command todo is the todo application's CLI: a cobra command tree over the
// Turso store. The tree itself lives in internal/cli; this file is the
// wiring — signals, the real opener, the process logger, and the exit code.
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"path/filepath"
	"syscall"

	"golang.org/x/term"

	"todo/internal/cli"
	"todo/internal/config"
	"todo/internal/logging"
	"todo/internal/store"
)

// main is the process's only job: exit with run's code.
func main() {
	os.Exit(run())
}

// run executes the command tree and returns the process's exit code: 0 on
// success, 1 after printing the one error line. It reads os.Args and writes
// to os.Stdout and os.Stderr, so the real binary and testscript's
// re-executed test binary — which needs a func() int to call — run the same
// function.
func run() int {
	// A first interrupt or SIGTERM cancels ctx, so every store call aborts
	// with a context error instead of the process dying mid-write. stop
	// unregisters the handler; the defer covers the normal return, while
	// main's os.Exit skips it — the process is leaving anyway.
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	// The logger must exist before the tree runs — every command takes it —
	// so the log path is resolved here, before cobra has seen any flag. The
	// database path this Load also produces is discarded: the tree resolves
	// again in its pre-run with --db, the flag this function cannot see yet.
	// The log path does not depend on --db, so the two resolutions agree on
	// it.
	cfg, err := config.Load(os.Getenv, "")
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}

	// The TTY decision belongs here, where the real stderr is: a terminal
	// gets tint's human-readable records, anything else JSON — machines
	// parse. The file sink is JSON either way.
	isTTY := term.IsTerminal(int(os.Stderr.Fd()))
	logger, closer, err := logging.New(os.Stderr, isTTY, cfg.LogPath, slog.LevelInfo)
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	defer func() {
		// The process is leaving; a close error cannot change the exit
		// code and has nowhere better to go, so it is discarded
		// explicitly, like the import handle in the CLI.
		_ = closer.Close()
	}()

	// The CLI owns the store's lifecycle now: it resolves the path, calls
	// openStore, and runs the returned cleanup when the command finishes.
	// main does not close the store itself — that defer from chapter 25
	// would close the handle a second time on the success path.
	root := cli.New(openStore, logger, os.Stdout, os.Stderr)
	if err := root.ExecuteContext(ctx); err != nil {
		// The tree silences cobra's own error reporting, so this is the one
		// place an error is printed: once, on stderr, the way a Unix tool
		// reports it. It is deliberately not logged as well: the one line
		// and the exit code are the error contract, and a second copy would
		// be noise.
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
		return 1
	}
	return 0
}

// openStore is the production OpenFunc: it opens the Turso store at the
// path the CLI resolved and hands the store's Close back as the cleanup.
// The resolved path's parent may not exist yet — the XDG default nests
// todo/ under $XDG_DATA_HOME — so the opener creates it first; the path's
// location is configuration's decision, and making it real is the opener's.
func openStore(ctx context.Context, dbPath string) (store.Store, func() error, error) {
	if err := os.MkdirAll(filepath.Dir(dbPath), 0o700); err != nil {
		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("open store: %w", err)
	}
	st, err := store.NewTursoStore(ctx, dbPath)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, err
	}
	return st, st.Close, nil
}
````


## `cmd/todo/main_test.go`

````go
// The binary's black-box tests live in package main: TestMain builds the
// real binary once for the exec.Command tests and registers the binary's
// main with testscript, so the txtar scenarios execute the same command
// tree a shell would — through a process boundary, with real exit codes.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/exec"
	"path/filepath"
	"runtime"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/rogpeppe/go-internal/testscript"
)

// commands is the testscript command table: main, under the name the
// scripts exec, so a scripted `todo` is exactly what the binary runs —
// os.Exit(run()). TestMain reads the map to tell a re-executed command from
// the top-level `go test` process, which is the only one with a module to
// build.
var commands = map[string]func(){"todo": main}

// binPath is the CLI binary TestMain builds once for the exec.Command tests
// in integration_test.go; binDir is the temporary directory holding it,
// removed after the suite.
var (
	binPath string
	binDir  string
)

// TestMain builds the real binary once and then hands the suite to
// testscript.Main — the testscript contract for in-process commands.
// Main decides whether this process is `go test` or a re-executed command:
// in the first case it registers commands, runs the tests through suite,
// and exits; in the second it calls the command function, which exits with
// run's code. The build runs only in the first case, because a script's
// `exec todo` starts this binary with the script's work directory as its
// working directory, where there is nothing to build.
func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
	if !isCommandInvocation() {
		if err := buildBinary(); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
			os.Exit(1)
		}
	}
	testscript.Main(suite{m}, commands)
}

// suite adapts *testing.M for testscript.Main. Main always leaves through
// os.Exit, so the wrapper's Run is the last code before that exit — the
// place to remove the built binary's directory.
type suite struct {
	m *testing.M
}

// Run runs the tests, removes the binary's directory, and returns the exit
// code for Main to exit with.
func (s suite) Run() int {
	code := s.m.Run()
	if binDir != "" {
		if err := os.RemoveAll(binDir); err != nil {
			fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "remove test binary dir:", err)
		}
	}
	return code
}

// isCommandInvocation reports whether this process was re-executed as one
// of the commands in commands rather than as `go test`. It mirrors Main's
// own detection rule, including the Windows .exe suffix.
func isCommandInvocation() bool {
	name := filepath.Base(os.Args[0])
	if runtime.GOOS == "windows" {
		name = strings.TrimSuffix(name, ".exe")
	}
	_, ok := commands[name]
	return ok
}

// buildBinary builds the CLI once for the whole suite. -cover instruments
// every package in the module, so a run with GOCOVERDIR set writes data
// `go tool covdata` reads back — TestBinary_Coverage's subject. One build
// serves every black-box test; rebuilding per test would dominate the
// suite's runtime.
func buildBinary() error {
	dir, err := os.MkdirTemp("", "todo-bin-")
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("build test binary: %w", err)
	}
	binDir = dir
	binPath = filepath.Join(dir, "todo")
	// `go test` runs this binary with the package directory as the working
	// directory, so `.` is cmd/todo.
	// #nosec G204 -- the command is a literal; only the output path, chosen
	// right here, varies.
	cmd := exec.Command("go", "build", "-cover", "-o", binPath, ".")
	cmd.Stderr = os.Stderr
	if err := cmd.Run(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("build test binary: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

// TestScripts runs the scenarios under testdata/script. Each script drives
// `todo` through testscript's shell; `exec todo` re-executes this test
// binary, which testscript.Main routes to main.
func TestScripts(t *testing.T) {
	testscript.Run(t, testscript.Params{
		Dir: "testdata/script",
		// The engine extracts its native library on first open. testscript
		// runs every script under an unwritable HOME, so point the
		// extraction at the script's own work directory instead.
		Setup: func(env *testscript.Env) error {
			env.Setenv("TURSO_GO_CACHE_DIR", filepath.Join(env.WorkDir, ".turso-cache"))
			return nil
		},
	})
}
````

````text
# the only channel it uses for data — log records go to stderr. list logs
````

## `deploy/Caddyfile`

````text
# deploy/Caddyfile — the TLS front. Install to /etc/caddy/Caddyfile and
# `systemctl reload caddy` (see deploy/RUNBOOK.md).
#
# One site, one job: terminate TLS for the public name and proxy everything
# to the server's loopback socket. Caddy obtains and renews the certificate
# itself — ACME over ports 80 and 443, so the name must resolve to this host
# and those ports must be reachable — which is why nothing here names a
# certificate path.
#
# What Caddy does to the request on the way in is part of the app's contract,
# not an implementation detail:
#
#   - X-Forwarded-For is set from the connection, not from the request: a
#     client-supplied value is ignored by default (Caddy's documented
#     anti-spoofing default), so the server's right-to-left walk in
#     internal/api's IPExtractor sees the address Caddy saw. The walk is the
#     second layer: if a CDN is ever put in front (with the global
#     trusted_proxies option), the nearest untrusted hop is still the client
#     and the client's own prefix is still never read.
#   - X-Forwarded-Proto is https, which is what makes the server emit HSTS:
#     echo believes the header from a trusted peer, and the peer here is the
#     loopback socket the unit binds.
#   - The app sets its own security headers and its own CSP, and it compresses
#     its own responses; Caddy adds nothing and rewrites nothing. One layer
#     owns each decision.
#
# The scrape is the one thing the proxy closes. /metrics has no gate in the
# app — chapter 45's decision, made when the listen address was loopback: the
# body is counters and gauges with no task data, but route names, traffic
# volumes, and the runtime's own numbers are not the public site's business.
# The deployment is where that boundary is drawn, so it is drawn here: a
# scraper on the host reaches 127.0.0.1:8080 directly, and a remote one needs
# a deliberate exception in this file. The profiles need no line: the app
# already answers 401 to anyone without an admin session, and the API's spec
# and UI stay public on purpose — the shape of an API whose anonymous callers
# already get 401s is not a secret, and the UI is the page a client logs in
# through (see internal/api's New comment).
#
# The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only (see todo-server.service): this proxy is
# the only way in, which is what makes the trust rules above sound. Port 80
# is Caddy's automatic redirect to the https site, never the site itself, and
# the session cookie is Secure — a browser that somehow received it over http
# would never send it back.

todo.example.com {
	@internals path /metrics
	respond @internals 404

	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
}
````


## `deploy/Dockerfile`

````dockerfile
# deploy/Dockerfile — the release image: the server binary on a distroless
# base, nothing else. GoReleaser builds it from the binaries it already
# built; this file copies one into place. The name is deploy/Dockerfile
# because the image is deployment material, next to the unit it is the
# container-shaped alternative to.
#
# The base is distroless's `base`, not `static`, and that is chapter 20's
# finding cashed in: CGO_ENABLED=0 removes the C toolchain from the build,
# not libc from the runtime — purego resolves libc/libdl dynamically to load
# the Turso engine, so an image without a libc cannot open the store.
# `base` has the glibc the driver needs; `static` would fail at the first
# store open. (`base` also carries ca-certificates, for the OTLP exporter,
# and /tmp, which is writable — the engine's extraction cache lives there.)
#
# The throwaway stage makes the data directory. distroless has no shell, so
# `RUN mkdir` cannot happen in the final image; and the directory has to
# exist there with the right ownership, because a fresh named volume is
# seeded from the image's own path — with its ownership — on first mount.
# Without it, `docker run -v todo-data:/data` would hand the server a
# root-owned volume it cannot write. The ownership is spelled on the copy
# itself: the nonroot user distroless defines is uid 65532, and the file
# inside keeps the copied directory from being an empty-directory edge
# case. (Nothing here can be built on this machine — no container runtime —
# which is why the flag is explicit rather than inferred from a build.)
FROM debian:12-slim AS data
RUN install -d /data && touch /data/.volume

FROM gcr.io/distroless/base-debian12:nonroot

ARG TARGETPLATFORM
COPY --from=data --chown=65532:65532 /data /data
COPY $TARGETPLATFORM/todo-server /usr/local/bin/todo-server

# The engine extracts its native library on first open — a cache, so the
# container's ephemeral /tmp is exactly the right place — and the database
# is a file on the volume. TODO_LISTEN binds every interface of the
# container's own network namespace, which is the boundary here; the unit's
# loopback default exists because Caddy shares the host with it, and a
# container's neighbors do not. The admin key is the operator's secret to
# mount and name (TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE); a container without one serves, and
# has no admin, exactly like a server without one.
ENV TURSO_GO_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/turso-go \
    TODO_DB=/data/todo.db \
    TODO_LOG=/data/todo.log \
    TODO_LISTEN=:8080

VOLUME ["/data"]
EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/todo-server"]
````


## `deploy/RUNBOOK.md`

````markdown
# Runbook — deploying the todo server

One binary, one systemd unit, one Caddy site, one backup timer. The shape:

```text
client ──TLS──> Caddy :443 ──http──> 127.0.0.1:8080 (todo-server) ──> /var/lib/todo/todo.db
                     │                        (DynamicUser, StateDirectory, LoadCredential)
                     └── ACME (ports 80/443)          ▲
                                                      │
                              /usr/local/lib/todo/todo-backup ── todo-backup.timer (daily)
```

The artifacts this runbook installs, all in `deploy/`:
`todo-server.service` · `todo-backup.sh` · `todo-backup.service` ·
`todo-backup.timer` · `Caddyfile`. Every command below is what the deploy
workflow (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`) does over ssh; the manual path is
the same path.

## Install

1. **The binaries.** From the repository:

   ```sh
   CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o todo-server ./cmd/todo-server
   CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -o todo      ./cmd/todo
   sudo install -m 0755 todo-server todo /usr/local/bin/
   ```

   The CLI is not decoration: the backup job verifies its copies with it.

2. **The units and the backup job.**

   ```sh
   sudo install -m 0644 deploy/todo-server.service \
       deploy/todo-backup.service deploy/todo-backup.timer /etc/systemd/system/
   sudo install -D -m 0755 deploy/todo-backup.sh /usr/local/lib/todo/todo-backup
   sudo install -D -m 0644 deploy/RUNBOOK.md /usr/local/share/doc/todo/RUNBOOK.md
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
   ```

3. **Caddy.** Install Caddy for your distribution, then:

   ```sh
   sudo install -m 0644 deploy/Caddyfile /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
   sudoedit /etc/caddy/Caddyfile        # replace todo.example.com with your name
   sudo systemctl reload caddy
   ```

   The site name must resolve to this host and ports 80 and 443 must be
   reachable: Caddy gets the certificate itself (ACME) and renews it.

4. **The deploy account**, if the workflow will deploy. An account with
   `sudo` for `install` and `systemctl restart todo-server` — nothing else:

   ```sh
   sudo -u deploy ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -N '' -f ~deploy/.ssh/deploy_key
   # the private key becomes the DEPLOY_SSH_KEY secret
   ssh-keyscan -H todo.example.com | sudo tee -a ~deploy/.ssh/known_hosts
   # that line becomes the DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS secret
   ```

   The workflow's four secrets live in the repository's `production`
   environment: `DEPLOY_HOST`, `DEPLOY_USER`, `DEPLOY_SSH_KEY`,
   `DEPLOY_KNOWN_HOSTS`. Add required reviewers to the environment and the
   dispatch button is gated by a human.

## First boot

1. **The admin credential.** Generate it once, keep a copy in the password
   manager, and let the file be the deployment's copy:

   ```sh
   openssl rand -base64 24          # store this value, then:
   sudo install -d -m 0750 /etc/todo
   printf '%s\n' '<the value>' | sudo tee /etc/todo/admin-key >/dev/null
   sudo chown root:root /etc/todo/admin-key
   sudo chmod 0400 /etc/todo/admin-key
   ```

   `LoadCredential=admin-key:/etc/todo/admin-key` copies it into the
   service's credential directory at mode 0400 on every start; the app never
   reads the source file. A world-readable source is refused by the boot
   (chapter 46), not silently accepted.

2. **The account it ensures.** The unit defaults `TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL` to
   `admin@example.com`. Override it without editing the unit — drop-ins are
   the supported way to make a packaged unit yours:

   ```sh
   sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/systemd/system/todo-server.service.d
   sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/todo-server.service.d/local.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF'
   [Service]
   Environment=TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com
   # Environment=TODO_OTEL_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:4318   # when a collector runs
   EOF
   sudo systemctl daemon-reload
   ```

3. **Start it, and read the boot record.**

   ```sh
   sudo systemctl enable --now todo-server
   systemctl status todo-server --no-pager
   journalctl -u todo-server -n 20 --no-pager
   ```

   The first boot logs `admin credential ensured` with `created:true` — the
   key became the account's password hash — then `server listening`. A boot
   that refuses the credential exits 1 before it serves anything.

4. **Through the front door.**

   ```sh
   curl -fsS https://todo.example.com/healthz      # {"status":"ok"}
   curl -fsS https://todo.example.com/ready        # pings the database
   ```

   Log in at `https://todo.example.com/login` with the admin email and the
   key. Sessions are `__Host-` cookies: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax.

## Day two

**Logs.** `journalctl -u todo-server -f` is the operational log, rotated by
journald; `/var/log/todo/todo.log` is the same records in JSON, 0600, for
tools — it has no rotation of its own, so a long-running host wants a
logrotate rule or `TODO_LOG=/dev/null` in a drop-in.

**Health and metrics.** `/healthz` (liveness) and `/ready` (readiness, pings
the database) are for the supervisor and the proxy; `/metrics` is the
Prometheus scrape. Profiles (`/debug/pprof`) sit behind an admin session and
are never public.

**Memory.** The unit caps the service at 256M:

```sh
systemctl show -p MemoryMax -p MemoryCurrent todo-server
systemd-cgtop -m
```

An OOM kill shows as a restart in the journal; the observed working set is
around 50–90 MiB, so a kill means something else grew.

**Backups.** The timer runs the job daily; a missed day (host down) runs at
the next boot (`Persistent=true`).

```sh
systemctl list-timers todo-backup.timer
sudo systemctl start todo-backup.service        # run one now
journalctl -u todo-backup.service -n 5 --no-pager
sudo ls -la /var/lib/todo/backups               # todo-<UTC stamp>.db
```

**Restore drill — do this once a quarter, on a scratch port.** A backup that
has never been opened is a hypothesis; this is the experiment. The copy holds
the admin account, and the key opens it — so the drill reads back the admin's
own list. (Other users' rows live in the same copy but not behind this key:
for a multi-user instance the drill proves the copy opens and serves, and the
suite's own restore check — a scoped store over the copy, in
`cmd/todo-server/backup_test.go` — is the shape to automate if a deployment
wants row counts per account.)

```sh
sudo systemctl stop todo-server
sudo install -m 0600 -o root -g root \
    /var/lib/todo/backups/todo-<stamp>.db /var/lib/todo/restore-drill.db
sudo env TODO_DB=/var/lib/todo/restore-drill.db TODO_LOG=/dev/null \
    TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.com TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE=/etc/todo/admin-key \
    /usr/local/bin/todo-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8081
# in another shell: log in at http://127.0.0.1:8081/login with the key and
# compare the task list with what you expect. Then Ctrl-C — the first signal
# drains — and:
sudo rm /var/lib/todo/restore-drill.db
sudo systemctl start todo-server
```

What the drill proves: the copy opens, its schema is current, and the rows
the server held are there. What the job's own verification already proves on
every run: the copy opens and is not torn (see the comment at the top of
`todo-backup.sh` for why that is not the same thing).

**Upgrade.**

```sh
sudo cp /usr/local/bin/todo-server /usr/local/bin/todo-server.prev
# build, then:
sudo install -m 0755 todo-server /usr/local/bin/todo-server
sudo systemctl restart todo-server
journalctl -u todo-server -n 10 --no-pager    # "shutting down" → "server stopped"
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/ready
```

The restart is a SIGTERM: the old process drains in-flight requests (its
budget is 15s, then the tracer's 5s flush; the unit's `TimeoutStopSec=25s`
outlasts both) and exits 0. If a drain ever hangs, a second SIGTERM from a
terminal ends the process — and systemd's own SIGKILL after
`TimeoutStopSec` is the last resort.

**Rollback.** Binary regressions: install `todo-server.prev` back and
restart. Schema is forward-only — an older binary against a newer schema is
not a rollback, it is a downgrade, and the migrations do not promise it.

**Secrets.** Rotating the admin key is chapter 46's one step: write the new
value to `/etc/todo/admin-key`, `systemctl restart todo-server`, and the boot
records `rotated:true` — old key stops working, live sessions survive. The
deploy key rotates by replacing the `DEPLOY_SSH_KEY` secret and the matching
`authorized_keys` line.

## What the workflow runs

`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` is dispatched by hand (or by `gh workflow run
deploy`), takes a `ref`, and runs the same steps above: `make check` on the
exact ref, a `CGO_ENABLED=0` build, the key install, `scp`, the remote
`install` + `systemctl restart`, and a `/ready` check through the loopback.
It takes effect once a remote and the environment's
secrets exist.
````


## `deploy/todo-backup.service`

````ini
# deploy/todo-backup.service — the backup job's unit; deploy/todo-backup.timer
# starts it daily. Install both, then `systemctl enable --now
# todo-backup.timer` (see deploy/RUNBOOK.md).
#
# The job runs as root because it must read a state directory that belongs to
# the server's dynamic user — an identity that changes per boot, so no fixed
# user could own the read. It writes exactly one directory (the copies) and
# nothing else: ProtectSystem=strict makes the rest of the filesystem
# read-only, and ReadWritePaths is the one exception. A failed run stays
# failed (no Restart): the timer will try again tomorrow, and the journal and
# the exit status are where a human looks — a retry loop that hides a
# verification failure would be worse than the failure.

[Unit]
Description=Back up the todo database
Documentation=file:/usr/local/share/doc/todo/RUNBOOK.md

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/lib/todo/todo-backup
Environment=TODO_DB=/var/lib/todo/todo.db
Environment=TODO_BACKUP_DIR=/var/lib/todo/backups
Environment=TODO_BIN=/usr/local/bin/todo
MemoryMax=256M
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/todo
PrivateTmp=yes
NoNewPrivileges=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
````


## `deploy/todo-backup.sh`

````bash
#!/bin/sh
# deploy/todo-backup.sh — the database's backup job, run by todo-backup.timer
# and runnable by hand. See deploy/RUNBOOK.md for the install and the restore
# drill.
#
# The database is one file with sidecars, and the sidecars are the point:
# under MVCC the committed rows live in <db>-log until a checkpoint folds
# them into <db> (see internal/store's Close and notes/deploy.md), and the
# engine holds the files open for the server process's lifetime — a second
# process cannot open, checkpoint, or copy them through SQL while the server
# runs. The job is therefore a file copy, and a copy of <db> alone is missing
# everything written since the last checkpoint: it opens perfectly well (the
# migrations rebuild an empty schema) and holds nothing.
#
# Order: the main file first, then every sidecar. The main file only advances
# at a checkpoint; the log only grows between checkpoints. A copy taken
# db-first is therefore either current (log appended since) or consistent but
# a checkpoint old (log truncated under it) — never a log applied to the
# wrong database. Sidecars-first would risk exactly that: a log read before a
# checkpoint, then a main file read after it, restores a stale delta onto a
# newer file.
#
# Verification: the copy is opened with the application itself ($TODO_BIN,
# the CLI) — a torn copy fails there and is discarded — and the
# verification's own open folds the sidecars into the copy, so what is left
# in the backup directory is one portable .db file. The check proves the copy
# opens and its schema is current; it cannot prove the copy is current (the
# source is locked, so nothing can compare) and it does not read the owned
# rows (the CLI's list is the user-less scope) — counting rows is the restore
# drill's job.
#
# Environment (the unit sets all of these; the defaults are the unit's paths):
#   TODO_DB           the live database path
#   TODO_BACKUP_DIR   where the copies go
#   TODO_BIN          the todo CLI used for the verification
#   TODO_BACKUP_KEEP  how many copies to keep, newest first
set -eu

DB=${TODO_DB:-/var/lib/todo/todo.db}
DIR=${TODO_BACKUP_DIR:-/var/lib/todo/backups}
BIN=${TODO_BIN:-/usr/local/bin/todo}
KEEP=${TODO_BACKUP_KEEP:-14}

umask 077
mkdir -p "$DIR"

stamp=$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
dest=$DIR/todo-$stamp.db

if [ ! -f "$DB" ]; then
	echo "todo-backup: $DB does not exist" >&2
	exit 1
fi

cp -- "$DB" "$dest"
if [ -e "$DB-log" ]; then cp -- "$DB-log" "$dest-log"; fi
if [ -e "$DB-wal" ]; then cp -- "$DB-wal" "$dest-wal"; fi
if [ -e "$DB-shm" ]; then cp -- "$DB-shm" "$dest-shm"; fi

# The verification must not write a second log file beside the backups:
# TODO_LOG is set to /dev/null, the CLI's log sink is resolved on every run,
# and the copy's own records are the backup's business, not the CLI's.
if ! TODO_LOG=/dev/null "$BIN" --db "$dest" list --json >/dev/null; then
	echo "todo-backup: $dest failed verification; discarding" >&2
	rm -f "$dest" "$dest-log" "$dest-wal" "$dest-shm"
	exit 1
fi

echo "todo-backup: wrote $dest"

# Keep the newest $KEEP copies. The sidecars are removed too in case a copy
# never reached the verification's fold.
ls -1t "$DIR"/todo-*.db 2>/dev/null | tail -n +"$((KEEP + 1))" | while IFS= read -r old; do
	rm -f "$old" "$old-log" "$old-wal" "$old-shm"
done
````


## `deploy/todo-backup.timer`

````ini
# deploy/todo-backup.timer — the backup's schedule.
#
# Persistent=true is the one line that matters on a machine that is not up at
# midnight: a missed run happens at the next boot instead of being skipped.
# The randomized delay keeps every host that installed this unit from hitting
# its disk at the same instant, and AccuracySec gives systemd room to batch
# the wakeup with others. The cadence is daily because the database is one
# file of a personal task list: a day of loss is the worst case, and the
# copies are kept two weeks (TODO_BACKUP_KEEP in deploy/todo-backup.sh).

[Unit]
Description=Daily backup of the todo database
Documentation=file:/usr/local/share/doc/todo/RUNBOOK.md

[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
RandomizedDelaySec=30m
AccuracySec=1m
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
````


## `deploy/todo-server.service`

````ini
# deploy/todo-server.service — the server as a systemd service.
#
# Install to /etc/systemd/system/todo-server.service; deploy/RUNBOOK.md walks
# the install, the credential, and the first boot. Every promise here is one
# of the binary's own facts: the listen address is the loopback socket Caddy
# proxies to (see deploy/Caddyfile), the signal it drains on is SIGTERM (see
# cmd/todo-server), and the credential it loads is the file internal/secret
# verifies at mode 0400.
#
# The unit is the deployment's boundary, so the sandbox is written out rather
# than left to defaults: the process gets a dynamic identity, no capabilities,
# no home, a read-only filesystem except the directories systemd makes
# writable for it, and a memory ceiling. systemd-analyze security scores it in
# the dry run (see notes/deploy.md); the threshold lives in the Makefile's
# deploy-check.

[Unit]
Description=Todo API and web server
Documentation=file:/usr/local/share/doc/todo/RUNBOOK.md
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=exec
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/todo-server --listen 127.0.0.1:8080

# Identity and state. DynamicUser allocates a uid at start and releases it at
# stop: no account to create, no home, nothing to leak into a shell. The two
# directories are the process's whole writable world — StateDirectory=todo is
# /var/lib/todo for the database, LogsDirectory=todo is /var/log/todo for the
# log file — and they are what keeps ProtectSystem=strict from being a
# promise the process cannot keep.
DynamicUser=yes
StateDirectory=todo
StateDirectoryMode=0700
LogsDirectory=todo
Environment=TODO_DB=/var/lib/todo/todo.db
Environment=TODO_LOG=/var/log/todo/todo.log

# The admin credential. LoadCredential copies /etc/todo/admin-key — the
# operator's file, root-owned — into the service's credentials directory,
# owned by the service user and mode 0400; %d is that directory, so the
# process reads the copy and never the source. internal/secret accepts 0400
# unchanged and refuses anything group- or other-readable (chapter 46), so a
# misconfigured source fails the boot with the mode named instead of a silent
# rotation. TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL names the account the key ensures; it is the one
# setting a deployment overrides (see the runbook's drop-in).
LoadCredential=admin-key:/etc/todo/admin-key
Environment=TODO_ADMIN_EMAIL=admin@example.com
Environment=TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE=%d/admin-key

# Memory. MemoryMax is the cgroup's hard ceiling: the kernel OOM-kills the
# service if it exceeds it, and Restart=on-failure below brings it back. The
# number is measured, not guessed: the dry run measured 76–87 MiB of resident
# set with the engine's page cache warm (cgroup memory.current ~48–51 MiB;
# see notes/deploy.md), so 256M is roughly 3x the observed peak.
#
# GOMEMLIMIT is the runtime's half of the same bound: a soft heap ceiling.
# As the heap approaches it the collector works harder instead of letting
# the heap grow, so the process slows down under memory pressure instead of
# being killed for it — the kernel's OOM kill is not a plan. The number is
# measured (chapter 50's notes): the hundred-thousand-task read ran unchanged
# with the limit at 128MiB — 1.709 s against 1.711 s, p=0.84 — while the
# process's peak resident set stayed at 179 MiB against 799 MiB uncapped.
# 192MiB sits under the unit's 256M hard ceiling with room for the engine's
# native memory, which no Go limit covers. The same measurement says what
# *not* to do here: raising GOGC to make the collector run less often bought
# no time on the read path (it was 3% slower) and cost 328 MiB of resident
# set against 156 MiB. The collector's cost is not on that path.
MemoryMax=256M
Environment=GOMEMLIMIT=192MiB

# Lifecycle. SIGTERM is systemd's default kill signal and is named here
# because the binary's drain semantics depend on it: the first signal drains,
# bounded by the process's own budget, and a second one ends it outright.
# TimeoutStopSec must outlast everything the process does on the way out or
# systemd's SIGKILL would cut it: the drain (15s), the tracer's flush (5s,
# after the drain), and a margin — 25s. Restart brings the service back after
# a crash or an OOM kill; a clean stop is exit 0 and is not restarted.
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5s
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=25s

# Sandbox. Each line removes a door the process does not use; the runbook's
# day-two section names the ones to revisit if the process ever grows one
# (AF_UNIX for a unix socket, a device, a kernel tunable).
NoNewPrivileges=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
AmbientCapabilities=
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectProc=invisible
ProcSubset=pid
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM
UMask=0077

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
````


## `docs/threat-model.md`

````markdown
# Threat model

This is the audit's document: what the application protects, who can reach
it, where the trust boundaries are, and which threats the controls answer.
The mapping is to OWASP ASVS 5.0, in the four chapters this application's
surface lives in: **V4 API and Web Service**, **V6 Authentication**, **V7
Session Management**, **V8 Authorization**. The machine-checked half of the
audit lives beside it — `govulncheck`, `gitleaks`, the dependency allowlist
and the bill of materials (`internal/audit`), the lint config — and this
document is the human half: the decisions those tools cannot read.

It is a snapshot of the tree the `audit` checkpoint names. It is not a
compliance claim: every requirement below is marked *met*, *partial*, *gap*,
or *n/a* with a reason, and the gaps are listed rather than glossed. The
deployment chapter (48) moves some boundaries — TLS, the proxy, systemd's
credentials — and those moves are named where they land.

## The system and its boundaries

Three binaries share one domain: `todo` (CLI), `todo-server` (JSON API and
server-rendered pages on one echo instance), `todo-tui` (an API client). The
server is one process over one SQLite-compatible database file (Turso, no
cgo). The boundaries, from the outside in:

1. **The network.** The server binds `127.0.0.1:8080` by default — loopback
   until an operator says otherwise (`internal/config`). The process speaks
   plain HTTP; TLS, the public listener, and the proxy are the deployment's
   (chapter 48). HSTS is emitted only when the request's scheme is https,
   and echo believes a forwarded scheme only from a trusted peer
   (`internal/api/middleware.go`).
2. **The browser session.** One `__Host-session` cookie carries a reference
   token; the form edge adds a per-session CSRF token. The JSON edge relies
   on the cookie policy plus the same-origin stance (`internal/web/csrf.go`).
3. **The operator.** The first admin arrives through `TODO_ADMIN_KEY` (or
   `TODO_ADMIN_KEY_FILE`), loaded before anything opens a file and stored as
   an argon2id hash; systemd's `LoadCredential=` is the same file with a
   stricter mode (chapter 46, chapter 48).
4. **The database file.** Local, unencrypted, and the whole state: task
   rows, password hashes, hashed session tokens, the audit trail. Anyone who
   can read the file reads task data and material to crack, not credentials
   to replay.
5. **The repository and the supply chain.** The history is forever
   (`make leaks`); the module graph is allowlisted and inventoried
   (`internal/audit`, `docs/sbom.cdx.json`); tools are pinned as
   `go run …@version` (Makefile).
6. **The process's own memory.** Logs and profiles: the profiles sit behind
   `RequireUser` and `RequireAdmin` because memory can hold anything
   (`internal/api/api.go`); log records are built from an attribute
   discipline and a redacting type (`internal/secret`).

## Assets

| Asset | Where it lives | What protects it |
|---|---|---|
| Task data | `tasks` rows | ownership scoping in the queries; foreign reads answer 404 |
| Password hashes | `users.password_hash` (PHC argon2id) | one-way hash; never serialized; `grep -rn 'Reveal()'` audits the exits |
| Admin key | operator's environment / file / systemd credential | owner-only mode bits; argon2id hash at rest; `secret.Secret` redaction; never in `Config` |
| Session tokens | cookie (reference token) and `sessions` table (SHA-256 digest) | `__Host-` prefix, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax; 24 h absolute lifetime; renewed at login |
| CSRF token | session payload | one per session; constant-time compare; rotated with the session at login |
| Audit trail | `audit_events` | written in the same transaction as the change it records; never rewritten |
| Log records | stderr (tint/JSON) and the XDG state file | no secrets by type; request and trace ids for correlation |
| Profiles | `/debug/pprof` | `RequireUser` + `RequireAdmin`, flag read per request |
| Supply chain | `go.mod`, `go.sum`, allowlist, SBOM | `govulncheck`, `gitleaks`, the allowlist test, the SBOM test, pinned tools |

## Actors

- **Anonymous caller** — can reach the health endpoints, the auth routes,
  the spec and its UI, and every refusal.
- **Registered user** — owns their tasks; every store view is scoped to
  them; no user can read or write another's tasks.
- **Admin** — a user with the flag; reaches the profiles. The flag is read
  from the database on every gated request, so a grant or revoke lands on
  the next request.
- **Local operator** — shell access to the machine: sets the key, runs the
  CLI's `admin grant`, can read the database file. Outside the process's
  trust boundary by construction; the app's job is to leave them as little
  as possible (a hash, not a key).
- **A reader of a stolen copy** — the database file, a log file, a clone of
  the history. The design goal: a copy yields material to crack and data to
  read, but no credential to replay and no secret to harvest.
- **The dependency ecosystem** — every module in the graph is code that runs
  in this process.

## Threats and controls

| Threat | Control | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Credential stuffing, brute force | one token bucket per source address, shared by both login edges; every attempt costs ~19 ms of argon2id | `internal/api/ratelimit.go`; `TestLoginLimiter_OneBudgetAcrossEdges`, `TestLoginLimiter_429` |
| Account enumeration | one sentinel for both failures; an unknown email is verified against a dummy hash so timing matches | `internal/auth/auth.go`; `TestLogin_WrongPassword`, `TestLogin_EmptyCredentials` |
| Session theft | reference token, digest at rest, `__Host-` + Secure + HttpOnly + SameSite=Lax, fixed 24 h lifetime | `internal/api/sessions.go`, `internal/auth/session.go`; `TestSessionCookie_HostPrefix`, `TestSessionStore_HashesTokenAtRest` |
| Session fixation | the token is re-issued at login; the CSRF token rotates with it | `internal/api/auth.go`; `TestLogin_RenewsSessionAndCSRFToken` |
| IDOR / BOLA (a foreign task) | the scope lives in the queries; a foreign id answers exactly what a missing id answers | `internal/api/authorization.go`; `TestTask_Foreign_Returns404` |
| Privilege escalation to the profiles | `RequireAdmin` reads the flag from the database per request; an authenticated non-admin gets a named 403 | `internal/api/authorization.go`; `TestPprof_RequiresAdmin` |
| CSRF on the form edge | synchronizer token, constant-time compare, refusal before any handler runs | `internal/web/csrf.go`; `TestCSRF_LoginFormCarriesTheToken` |
| XSS | no JavaScript anywhere; templ escapes by construction; CSP `script-src 'none'` (the docs UI has its own, confined policy) | `internal/api/middleware.go`; `TestCSP_Snapshot`, `TestCSP_SwaggerUI`, `TestIndexPage_RendersTasks` |
| Clickjacking | `frame-ancestors 'none'` and `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, pinned together | `TestSecurityHeaders` |
| MIME sniffing | `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`; every response names its type | `TestSecurityHeaders`, `internal/web/web.go` |
| Request-body DoS | 64 KiB body limit (Content-Length and a counting reader), 10 s deadline, gzip threshold, 64-char request-id cap | `internal/api/middleware.go`; `TestTimeout_504`, `TestCreateTask_UnusableBody` |
| Header spoofing | the limiter keys on the transport peer, not `RealIP`; forwarded headers are trusted only from trusted peers | `internal/api/ratelimit.go`; `TestHSTS` |
| Panic as an outage or leak | `Recover` returns the error into the one handler; the stack stays in the process | `TestPanic_Recovered` |
| Error-message leakage | one JSON error shape; internal failures log their text and answer a fixed message | `internal/api/error.go` |
| Unreadiness misreported as health | `/healthz` touches nothing; `/ready` pings the store and answers 503 | `TestHealthz`, `TestReady_StoreDown` |
| Secret in a log, a string, or a document | `secret.Secret` closes `String`, `GoString`, `LogValue`, `MarshalText`; one `Reveal` exit | `internal/secret`; `TestSecret_Redacts`, `TestSecret_ProcessLogger` |
| Secret in the git history | `gitleaks` over every commit, in the gate and in CI (deep checkout) | `make leaks`; clean over the full history (the count moves with every commit) |
| Vulnerable dependency | `govulncheck` over the module; the finding it reports at module level is unreachable code | `make vulncheck`; 0 vulnerabilities found, 1 module-level advisory not called |
| Rogue direct dependency | the allowlist test refuses a direct requirement with no documented reason | `internal/audit`; `TestDependenciesAreAllowlisted` |
| Stale bill of materials | the SBOM test checks the committed document against `go.mod` in both directions | `internal/audit`; `TestSBOMNamesEveryRequirement` |
| Undocumented lint suppression | every `#nosec` must carry its reason; generated files are excluded | `internal/audit`; `TestSuppressionsCarryReasons` |
| Lost update / stale write | version compare-and-swap on every write; a stale snapshot is a 409 | `internal/store`; `TestConcurrentUpdates_Conflict` |
| Corrupt import / half-written export | atomic export write; bounded, transactional import | `TestWriteExportFile_FailedWriteKeepsOldFile`, `TestImportJSON_Atomic` |

## ASVS 5.0 mapping

Status: **met** (control present and tested), **partial** (present with a
named limitation), **gap** (absent; listed in Residual risks), **n/a** (the
mechanism does not exist here). Levels follow ASVS 5.0's own; the
application claims full L1 coverage and names its L2/L3 gaps rather than
implying them.

### V4 API and Web Service

| ID | Requirement (short) | Status | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4.1.1 | responses carry a Content-Type matching their content | met | echo's serializer (`application/json`); pages set `text/html; charset=utf-8` (`internal/web/web.go`); assets serve `text/css`; the error handler writes through `c.JSON` |
| 4.1.2 | only user-facing endpoints redirect http→https | n/a | nothing redirects; TLS belongs to the deployment (ch 48) |
| 4.1.3 | intermediary headers not overridable by the end user | met | the login limiter keys on the transport peer; echo's trusted-peer rule for forwarded headers (ch 48 owns the proxy configuration) |
| 4.1.4 | only explicitly supported methods | met | the route table is explicit; unused methods answer 405 in the one error shape (`codeForStatus`) |
| 4.1.5 | per-message digital signatures | n/a | no cross-system, high-value transactions |
| 4.2.1–4.2.4 | HTTP framing, smuggling, CRLF injection | met | `net/http` parses both edges; the application never re-frames messages and speaks one HTTP version |
````
